transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-09
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jenna Morris (Redwood AE), Carlos Ruiz (Redwood SE), Ava Chen (Blackrock Head of ML), Marco Silva (Blackrock Platform), Priya Natarajan (Blackrock Security), Ben Kim (Blackrock Data)

Summary:
Redwood gave a deep-dive demo of the Optimize console simulator focusing on concurrency controls, batching, and prefix/KV cache strategies. The session ran a few cost/vs-latency scenarios using Blackrock's sample traffic patterns. Key items: 1) recommendation for session-affinity + small batch sizes for sub-200ms SLO, 2) prefix-KV hits expected to reduce token spend on multi-turn workflows by ~28% in simulation, 3) reserved pool + burst for steady ingest, 4) security/compliance ask for KMS integration and audit log retention options.

Topics covered:
- Workload shape and tail latency sensitivity
- Batch sizing heuristics and concurrency limits
- Prefix vs session (KV) caching tradeoffs
- Cost-simulator assumptions (tokens, model variant, concurrency)
- Dedicated capacity vs hosted fallback policy
- Security: KMS, SSO, audit logs, data residency

Action items (quick):
- Jenna to share sandbox & simplified cost sheet
- Carlos to run a 24h sim on Blackrock sample traces
- Priya to confirm compliance artifact list

Transcript body:
[00:00:12] Jenna: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm jenna from Redwood, quick check — can you all see my screen?
[00:00:19] Ava: yep can see it, loud and clear. sorry i'm a few minutes late, trains, you know.
[00:00:27] Carlos: no worries, we'll kick off with the simulator then, i'll try to walk through three scenarios that match what you described in the brief — short chat queries, multi-turn support with user context, and high-throughput embedding-ish batch calls.
[00:00:41] Marco: sounds good, our main problem is unpredictable costs when the model keeps re-evaluating context — we think caching could help but worried about stale state and memory.
[00:00:52] Jenna: totally. quick orientation: the Optimize console sim uses your traffic histogram (tokens per request, turn length, concurrency) to run micro-sims. it models batching, prefix/KV cache, and session affinity together. results are cost per 1M requests and p95/p99 latency estimates.
[00:01:10] Priya: important for us — does that sim assume any particular encryption or KMS pattern? we need notes to feed to security.
[00:01:18] Carlos: by default we simulate compute + token costs. we also attach a KMS stub for key rotation overheads in the detailed run; i will add the explicit KMS integr details in the doc we share.
[00:01:30] Ava: great. i want to see the concrete savings numbers for multi-turn dialogues — some of our flows have a lot of short turns where the model re-requests the same prefix.
[00:01:42] Carlos: right, so first scenario — baseline: no caching, concurrency set to match your 200qps peak, model set to open-llama-13b-quant (heuristic near your production). in that run we get X tokens/1000 requests cost baseline, p95 about 220ms.
[00:02:02] Jenna: small note — the sim output calls out the effective batching window; if you keep concurrency low the runtime doesn't batch much, which raises per-token cost.
[00:02:12] Marco: question, how do you pick batch size in practice? we can't change user experience for latency-sensitive flows.
[00:02:19] Carlos: we recommend dynamic batching: set a max batch size (e.g., 8) and a short timeout (5-12ms) so interactive queries still flush quickly. for high-volume background calls you enable larger windows. dynamic batching pairs with session affinity so tokens that hit the cache avoid full decode.
[00:02:39] [00:02:40] Ben: when you say cache hit, is that prefix cache or KV cache? i'm not clear on the difference here.
[00:02:46] Jenna: good question — prefix cache is basically full prefix (n tokens) cached so subsequent continuations skip attention recompute; KV cache is per-layer key/value activations that let you resume generation without recomputing earlier positions. in practice we expose a prefix-friendly API abstraction and manage the low-level KV under the hood. sometimes docs call it session cache or lookahead cache — naming mismatch happens in other places.
[00:03:08] Ava: ok that naming is helpful. show us an example where prefix cache saves cost on a 6-turn dialog?
[00:03:16] Carlos: (switches tab) here's the sim: 6 turns, avg 16 tokens per turn user, 28 tokens assistant. baseline cost per 1k dialogs is $Y. with prefix cache enabled and a 70% hit rate (we estimated from your samples) cost drops ~28% — mostly from avoiding re-encoding the first 3-4 turns on each continuation.
[00:03:40] Marco: 70% hit rate is optimistic — our users sometimes vary their phrasing. how sensitive are these savings to hit rate?
[00:03:47] Carlos: great point — the sim has a sensitivity slider, lowering to 45% reduces measurable savings to about 12-14% but still non-trivial. we recommend focusing cache policies on stable prefixes (system prompts, onboarding text) rather than user freeform when possible.
[00:04:05] Priya: about stale state — do you provide TTL and invalidation controls? we can't have secret data persist forever.
[00:04:12] Jenna: yes, TTL per session + policy-based invalidation. we also support explicit cache invalidation via the Console or API. retention defaults are conservative; you can integrate with your KMS lifecycle.
[00:04:24] Ava: can you run a scenario where we prioritize latency (p95 < 150ms) versus cost? i want to know the tradeoffs.
[00:04:31] Carlos: sure. scenario two — low-latency SLO: we reduce max batch wait to 2ms, force smaller batches, keep session affinity on. result: p95 drops to 140ms but compute cost per 1k requests increases ~22%.
[00:04:50] Marco: that 22% is acceptable if it's predictable. how does dedicated capacity change this?
[00:04:56] Jenna: with Redwood Dedicated you can reserve GPU pools which gives predictable throughput; cost model shifts from per-token to fixed infra plus a smaller variable. Dedicated helps if you have steady high QPS. there's also a burst policy for peaks.
[00:05:09] Ben: one more metric — tail latency p99. we get timeouts during peaks and that's what's biting us in production.
[00:05:16] Carlos: the sim reports p99 too; caching helps p99 a lot because cache hits skip heavy compute, and batching smooths variance. we also model queueing for concurrency spikes. in your sample run enabling KV cache reduced p99 by about 180ms in the sim.
[00:05:34] Ava: can the system evict caches under memory pressure and still keep graceful degradation?
[00:05:40] Carlos: yes — eviction policies (LRU / priority by route) plus automatic fallback to smaller model variants if memory saturates. Redwood's routing can also fallback to a cheaper variant when Dedicated is tight.
[00:05:52] Priya: security question — if we use prefix cache with customer data, do you keep that cached data in our VPC or in Redwood-managed storage?
[00:06:01] Jenna: depends on deployment. Hosted: cached artifacts are encrypted at rest with customer keys (KMS) and we provide audit logs. Private or VPC deployments store cache within your network boundaries. we'll include an architectural note.
[00:06:15] Marco: great. also curious about costs when embeddings/batch jobs run in parallel, does the simulator mix job types?
[00:06:23] Carlos: we can simulate mixed workloads — embeddings, streaming chat, and batch generation. the key is to feed representative traffic. Ben, if you can share a 3-day sample trace we can run a realistic mixed-run.
[00:06:35] Ben: yeah i'll pull that and drop it in the secure share.
[00:06:40] [00:06:41] Ava: can you show the console where you configure cache policies? i want to see the controls.
[00:06:45] Carlos: (navigates) here — route map, per-route cache toggle, hit-rate estimators, TTL and per-layer retention. you can also pin route to dedicated pool, and set fallback to hosted or smaller variant.
[00:07:02] Jenna: note the "cost sensitivity" slider — it biases recommendations toward lower-cost profiles at the expense of a bit higher latency. you can tune it per environment.
[00:07:12] Marco: is there an API to run these sims? we want to automate nightly cost forecasts.
[00:07:18] Carlos: yes, there's a Sim API. it accepts traffic histogram and returns scenario outputs; we can give you an API key for sandbox.
[00:07:26] Priya: about compliance doc — do you have SOC2 type 2 and ISO attestation readily available?
[00:07:32] Jenna: yes, SOC2 Type II report, ISO docs, pen-test summary — i'll send the package. for KMS we have integration notes for AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and HSM options in private deployments.
[00:07:45] Ava: nice. can you also include an example mapping of our route names to policies? our infra team needs that.
[00:07:51] Jenna: yep i'll include a sample manifest.
[00:07:55] [00:08:05] Carlos: moving to scenario three — high-throughput background batches (embedding + rerank jobs). here we turn up batch window, allow large batch sizes, and disable prefix cache because embedding pipelines are stateless. this yields big per-token cost savings due to throughput efficiency.
[00:08:25] Marco: any gotchas with batching embeddings and chat on the same pool?
[00:08:30] Carlos: mixed workloads on the same pool can introduce jitter; we recommend separate pools or strict QoS routing. the console can define pool labels and route selectors.
[00:08:40] Ben: what about quantization effect — in sim you used a quantized model variant. how much of the cost comes from quantization vs cache?
[00:08:48] Carlos: both contribute; quantization reduces per-token compute cost substantially. cache reduces repeated work. we show breakdown — in your sample run quantization gave ~18% savings, cache ~28% (when hit-rate high). independent levers.
[00:09:06] Ava: can you annotate sim outputs with expected real-dollar numbers for our current pricing?
[00:09:12] Jenna: yes — we map to unit price assumptions; we'll include a simplified cost sheet with your numbers filled in.
[00:09:19] Marco: what about rollout — if we enable prefix cache in production, is there a canary path?
[00:09:25] Carlos: console supports canary rollouts by percentage and canary routes; you can monitor quality metrics and set automatic rollback on regressions.
[00:09:35] Priya: one last sec — audit logs retention options and export path? we need at least 1 year of request metadata.
[00:09:42] Jenna: audit logs are plumbed to S3/your logging endpoint, retention configurable. we'll include the retention SLA in the doc.
[00:09:52] Ava: ok great, this is helpful. can you summarize recommended first steps for us?
[00:09:58] Jenna: quick recap: 1) share sample traces (Ben) 2) Redwood runs a 24h sim with your traffic and returns a cost/latency breakdown (Carlos) 3) we provision sandbox with cache policies and an API key for automation (Jenna) 4) Security gets SOC2/KMS docs (Jenna) — timeline: sandbox creds by 2026-08-11, sim results by 2026-08-16.
[00:10:25] Ava: sounds good. i did want to probe deeper on one edge case — long-running streaming responses where KV cache isn't helpful because state is generated on the fly. any suggestions?
[00:10:34] Carlos: for streaming long responses we often use chunking + partial KV persist where feasible, and prioritize model variants tuned for streaming. plus we apply transient caches for the initial chunk to speed-up the early tokens. it's not perfect but reduces load.
[00:10:52] Ben: will the sim model streaming costs accurately?
[00:10:56] Carlos: we approximate streaming by token emit rate and model throughput; it's a good guide but we recommend a short live benchmark for final numbers.
[00:11:08] Priya: any network egress implications if we put cache in our VPC vs Redwood managed?
[00:11:14] Jenna: VPC private deployment keeps cache and inference in your subnet — egress minimal. hosted mode may incur egress depending on where your data origin is. we'll highlight that.
[00:11:26] Marco: okay that's helpful — one more operational ask: can the cache be instrumented in the Console per-route so we can see hit rates over time?
[00:11:33] Carlos: yes there's a hit-rate dashboard per route and a historical chart. we also emit metrics to Prometheus if you want to scrape.
[00:11:42] Ava: perfect. any immediate blockers from your side?
[00:11:45] Jenna: none. action items we already noted. we'll send the sandbox and docs and schedule a follow-up to review the sim outputs.
[00:11:55] [00:12:10] (brief cross talk about calendar slots)
[00:12:25] Marco: one practical question — when you recommend TTLs, is there a default that works across EU/US?
[00:12:31] Carlos: default is 24 hours for session cache; enterprise customers often set 1-7 days depending on compliance. for region-specific residency you can pin storage region.
[00:12:44] Ava: ok great. thank you all.
[00:12:48] Jenna: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in writing.

[End of capture — remaining ~40 minutes included detailed sim run artifacts shared offline]

Post-call notes (manual):
- Carlos ran the quick sim live and shared a link to the detailed CSV and charts (link: https://redwood.example/sim/ff-20260809-blackrock-001) — note link placeholder in transcript
- Estimated high-confidence recommendation: enable prefix cache for dialog routes that include system prompts + onboarding text, set TTL 24h, dynamic batching with max batch size 8 and short timeout for interactive flows, route heavy background batches to dedicated pool.
- Risk: if hit-rates are lower than estimated, savings shrink significantly. we recommended a staged rollout and short live A/B with telemetry on token spend per route.
